source: “HIST! Did you hear that noise, Cabaco?”

It was the middle-watch: a fair moonlight; the seamen were standing in a cordon, extending from one of the fresh-water butts in the waist, to the scuttle-butt near the taffrail. In this manner, they passed the buckets to fill the scuttle-butt. Standing, for the most part, on the hallowed precincts of the quarter-deck, they were careful not to speak or rustle their feet. From hand to hand, the buckets went in the deepest silence, only broken by the occasional flap of a sail, and the steady hum of the unceasingly advancing keel.
It was in the midst of this repose, that Archy, one of the cordon, whose post was near the after-hatches, whispered to his neighbor, a Cholo, the words above.
“Hist! did you hear that noise, Cabaco?”
“Take the bucket, will ye, Archy? what noise d’ye mean?”
“There it is again—under the hatches—don’t you hear it—a cough—it sounded like a cough.”
“Cough be damned! Pass along that return bucket.”
“There again—there it is!—it sounds like two or three sleepers turning over, now!”
“Caramba! have done, shipmate, will ye? It’s the three soaked biscuits ye eat for supper turning over inside of ye—nothing else. Look to the bucket!”
“Say what ye will, shipmate; I’ve sharp ears.”
“Aye, you are the chap, ain’t ye, that heard the hum of the old Quakeress’s knitting-needles fifty miles at sea from Nantucket; you’re the chap.”

“Grin away; we’ll see what turns up. Hark ye, Cabaco, there is somebody down in the after-hold that has not yet been seen on deck; and I suspect our old Mogul knows something of it too. I heard Stubb tell Flask, one morning watch, that there was something of that sort in the wind.”

modern_en.title: Chapter 43 — Hark!
paragraphs: "PSST! Did you hear that noise, Cabaco?"

It was the middle watch, in fair moonlight. The seamen were standing in a line stretching from one of the freshwater casks in the waist to the scuttlebutt (the drinking-water cask) near the taffrail. In this way they passed the buckets along to fill the scuttlebutt. Standing, for the most part, on the sacred ground of the quarter-deck, they were careful not to speak or shuffle their feet. From hand to hand the buckets went in the deepest silence, broken only by the occasional flap of a sail and the steady hum of the ceaselessly advancing keel.
It was in the middle of this calm that Archy, one of the line, whose station was near the after-hatches, whispered the words above to the man next to him, a Cholo.
"Psst! Did you hear that noise, Cabaco?"
"Take the bucket, will you, Archy? What noise do you mean?"
"There it is again — under the hatches — don't you hear it — a cough — it sounded like a cough."
"Cough be damned! Pass along that return bucket."
"There again — there it is! — it sounds like two or three sleepers turning over!"
"Caramba! Knock it off, shipmate, will you? It's the three soaked biscuits you ate for supper turning over inside you — nothing else. Watch the bucket!"
"Say what you want, shipmate. I've got sharp ears."
"Right, you're the one, aren't you, who heard the hum of the old Quaker lady's knitting needles fifty miles at sea from Nantucket. You're the one."

"Grin away. We'll see what turns up. Listen, Cabaco — there is somebody down in the after-hold who has not yet been seen on deck. And I suspect our old Mogul knows something about it too. I heard Stubb tell Flask, one morning watch, that there was something of that sort in the wind."
"Nonsense! The bucket!"

modern_da.title: Kapitel 43 — Hør!
paragraphs: »Psst! Hørte du den lyd, Cabaco?«

Det var midtvagten, i klart måneskin. Sømændene stod i en række fra et af ferskvandsfadene midtskibs til scuttlebutten (drikkevandsfadet) nær agterspejlet. På den måde sendte de spandene videre for at fylde scuttlebutten. De stod for det meste på agterdækkets hellige jord og passede på ikke at tale eller skrabe med fødderne. Fra hånd til hånd gik spandene i den dybeste tavshed, brudt kun af et sejls enkelte smæld og den jævne summen fra den uophørligt fremadskridende køl.
Det var midt i denne ro, at Archy, en af rækken, hvis plads var nær agterlugerne, hviskede ordene ovenfor til manden ved siden af sig, en cholo.
»Psst! Hørte du den lyd, Cabaco?«
»Tag spanden, vil du, Archy? Hvad for en lyd mener du?«
»Der er den igen — under lugerne — kan du ikke høre den — en hoste — det lød som en hoste.«
»Hoste, pokker i vold! Send den tomme spand videre.«
»Der igen — der er den! — det lyder som to eller tre sovende, der vender sig!«
»Caramba! Hold nu op, kammerat, vil du? Det er de tre udblødte skibskiks, du spiste til aftensmad, der vender sig inde i dig — ikke andet. Pas på spanden!«
»Sig, hvad du vil, kammerat. Jeg har skarpe ører.«
»Ja, du er jo den, der hørte summen af den gamle kvækerdames strikkepinde halvtreds engelske mil til søs fra Nantucket. Det er dig.«

»Grin bare. Vi får at se, hvad der dukker op. Hør, Cabaco — der er nogen dernede i agterlasten, som endnu ikke er blevet set på dækket. Og jeg har mistanke om, at vores gamle Mogul også ved noget om det. Jeg hørte Stubb sige til Flask en morgenvagt, at der var noget i den retning i luften.«
»Sludder! Spanden!«
